title: Say it out loud
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez challenges the maxim that actions speak louder than words, arguing that modeling behavior is not enough for leaders. Modeling only works when observers interpret it the way the leader intends, so without explanation people fill in the blanks themselves. She uses the analogy of a parent who eats vegetables without ever saying why, and extends it to organizations with multiple layers of management, where good behavior at the top may not filter down. Her prescription is concrete: name expectations, values and corrections aloud and repeatedly, and say the things people are afraid to ask, such as that a failure was not their fault. The central claim is that culture lives in articulation and clarity rather than assumption, and that clarity is among the greatest kindnesses a leader can give.
points: Leading by example is necessary but insufficient, because observers may not draw the conclusions the leader intends.
In multi-layer organizations, behaviors modeled at the top can be lost in translation, so leaders must check the filter is working.
Leaders should explicitly name what is valued and what is not, for instance rest over burnout, rather than leaning on ambiguous phrases about personal style.
Saying reassuring things aloud, such as that a failure was not the person's fault, opens space people are too afraid to request.
Culture that is felt but never named has not been solidified; repetition of stated expectations is part of the work.
quotes: Because the thing about modeling a behavior is that it only works when people are watching, interpreting, and drawing the same conclusions we are.

Let’s think about it in the context of our kids. We can eat vegetables in front of them all day, every single day, but if we never explicitly say, “We eat vegetables because they make us strong,” they could easily assume we just really like green stuff. They have no context, and therefore, they have no compelling reason to carry it forward.
Especially in the context of ambiguous (even if well-meaning) phrases such as, “We all have our own style of leadership.” In the absence of clarity, people fill in the blanks themselves.

It always helps me to think about it like a filter. Maybe all the right actions, behaviors, etc., are happening at the top, but are they trickling down? Are they making it through the filter, reaching the folks at the other end?
Sometimes, it’s about naming the stuff that people might not want to hear, but that they need to hear for the betterment of their leadership, their teams, and the organization at large.

Culture doesn’t live in assumption and implication; rather, it lives in articulation and clarity. We can’t just hope people pick up on how we expect others to lead, engage, and behave—we need to actually name it, over and over and over again.
One of the biggest kindnesses we can give in the world of leadership is clarity. We need to be the example—the change we wish to see. But also, we really need to say it out loud.
